conventions._: This file is the project's alignment prompt. Read it before writing an entry; it takes precedence over instinct about a placement. No script writes this file.
conventions.evidenceOrNothing: A lesson is recorded only when a specific ACTIVITY can be named and quoted. Topical similarity is not evidence. If no activity in the searched lessons asks students to do what the item asks, the honest entry is status 'no-lesson-found' with an empty evidence list -- that is a finding about the curriculum, not a failure of the process.
conventions.notATableLookup: Imagine Learning's Lessons by Standard table names the right UNIT 96.3% of the time but the right LESSON only 77.4% of the time, measured in provenance/alignment_baseline_measurement.md. Use it to choose the unit, then read every lesson the shortlist offers. Do not place an item at a lesson merely because the table lists it: that is the failure RegentsAlign's consistency audit traced to 'deferring to the official list'.
conventions.resolveByTitle: Resolve a lesson BY TITLE, never by number. Editions renumber; titles do not. Grades 7 and 8 swap Units 7 and 8 between the national and New York editions, and NYCPS's sheets use the national numbers.
conventions.homeGrade: A standard is searched in the grade that TEACHES it, not the grade of the test it appears on. Grade 8 items citing NY-7.G.2-G.6 are taught in the grade 7 curriculum; 20 items across the three grades are in this position.
conventions.severalLessonsIsNormal: An item may be taught in one lesson, practised in another and assessed in a third. Record each, with its own evidence and role. Forcing a single lesson destroys the answer to the question this project exists to answer.

roles.introduces: the activity where the idea or method first appears
roles.practises: an activity or practice problem applying it
roles.assessed: a Cool-down, section Checkpoint or End-of-Unit Assessment -- where the curriculum itself tests the skill

conventions.quoteLimit: Evidence quotes are at most 15 words. The teacher guides are licensed material; a citation plus a short quote is enough for a reader to find and check the activity, and preflight refuses to deploy a longer one.
conventions.draftMeansUnreviewed: Every entry is written with draft: true and is invisible to the site. build/payload.py skips drafted entries entirely, so a drafted entry cannot claim anything. Clearing the flag is the act of review, and is done by a person against the cited activity.
conventions.secondPass: A second pass RE-DERIVES the placement from the lessons rather than reviewing the first pass's prose. Reviewing prose finds typos; re-deriving finds wrong answers.

g8-2023-022.why: The item gives one interior angle of 34 degrees and asks which pair could be the other two; only the 180 degree sum separates 66 and 80 from the three distractors. Three Angles is the one place in the grade 7 curriculum that asks whether a given set of three angle measures can be a triangle at all: students try to draw 50/60/70, which works, and 50/60/100, which cannot be drawn, and then say whether either set determined a unique triangle. The first reading's Lesson 8, Triangles With 3 Common Measures, is the runner-up but asks a different question - it shows sets of triangles that already exist and asks how many of them are genuinely different (identical copies versus not) given the same three measures; it never asks whether three measures are possible. Home grade: NYSED tags this NY-7.G.2, so it is judged in the grade 7 curriculum, where the guide states outright that students are not expected to learn the 180 degree sum, though they are 'not barred from noticing' it - hence medium confidence. The rule itself is formalised in grade 8 Unit 1, Adding the Angles in a Triangle. New York edition numbering: grade 7's Unit 8 is Angles, Triangles, and Prisms, which is Unit 7 nationally.
